reading.rtitle: Open Call -- Care and Practice Residency 2027
paras: The Harbor Foundation invites artists to apply for three residencies of four months each, hosted by public hospitals in Lisbon, Rotterdam and Montreal. Each resident receives a monthly stipend of two thousand five hundred euros, a studio on the hospital grounds and a production budget. The residency is for artists whose practice engages with illness, care or the institutions of medicine. You do not have to be a medical professional, and you do not need a degree in the arts, but you must be able to show a track record of at least five years of independent work.

To be eligible, applicants must be at least twenty-five years old and must not be enrolled in a degree program during the residency. Applications must be submitted in English through the online portal by the deadline of March 15. Late or incomplete submissions will not be considered. A letter of support from a health institution is not required, but it is strongly recommended. Applicants who have held a Harbor residency in the last five years are not eligible.

Every submission must include a project proposal of no more than one thousand words, a portfolio of ten images or five minutes of video, and a budget. Applicants are expected to describe how they will work with patients and staff, and they should explain how consent will be obtained. Any project that involves recording patients is required to comply with the ethics policy of the host hospital. Failure to do so will disqualify the application at any stage.

Proposals will be assessed against three criteria: the quality of the artistic work, the relevance of the project to the host institution, and the care taken with the people involved. A panel of artists, clinicians and one former patient will shortlist ten applicants, who will be invited to an online interview in May. Successful applicants are expected to present their work at the end of the residency. Publishing a catalog is optional.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- B2 reading, written for this lesson as a realistic open call (the foundation and the residency are fictional)

listenings.text: I coordinate open calls for a residency program, and every year I read around four hundred applications. The first thing I want to say is simple: read the eligibility section twice. About one in ten applications is disqualified before anybody looks at the art, because the applicant is not eligible or a mandatory document is missing. The second thing is the difference between must and should. When a call says you must include a budget, it is not a suggestion. When it says you should include a letter of support, nobody will reject you without one, but the strongest applications usually have it. And when it says you do not have to have a degree, please believe it. Some of our best residents never went to art school. What we look for is a track record, a clear proposal, and evidence that you have thought about the people you will work with.

I sit on the panel for a hospital that hosts one artist every year, and I am the clinician in the room. I want to explain why our open call has so many rules about consent. When an artist records a patient, the patient is required to sign a form, and the artist is expected to explain, in plain language, what will happen to the recording. That is not bureaucracy. A patient on a ward is not in the same position as a visitor in a gallery. They cannot always leave, and they may feel they have to say yes. So when we shortlist applicants, one of our three criteria is care. We do not need a perfect ethics plan at that stage. We need to see that the artist has asked the right questions. An application that does not mention consent at all tells me the artist has not imagined the ward yet.
